title: The 5-Gigawatt Question: Tracking Data City’s Status as Its First Phase Deadline Approaches

content:
The world’s largest proposed data center hub — on 50,000 acres near Laredo — just got put on a global watchdog’s map. Today, Global Energy Monitor’s Oil and Gas Watch database, run with the Environmental Integrity Project, published a tracking page for the “Data City Energy Center” in Laredo, Webb County, Texas.

Here is what the new entry records, as of this morning:

  • Status: Announced
  • Fuel: Natural gas (fossil)
  • Capacity: 300 MW gas-turbine unit
  • Owner: Energy Abundance Development Corp (100%)
  • Start year (planned): 2026
  • Use: Captive power for a data center — not for the public grid

The tracker also notes that the project will be monitored for its environmental permit applications and construction status.

What the project claims

Energy Abundance Development Corp of Houston announced Data City, Texas as a 5-gigawatt, behind-the-meter data center campus powered by a blend of wind, solar, batteries, and dual-fuel gas turbines — running initially on Texas natural gas, shifting over time to green hydrogen stored in an adjacent 2-terawatt-hour salt-dome facility. The company’s stated target: a first phase of 300 MW and one million square feet of data center space, aimed at AI workloads on NVIDIA’s latest chips, launching in 2026.

With the year nearly over, the obvious question: has phase one broken ground? Webb Watch 956 has found no public evidence of construction, permit filings, or a formal application to the city or county. The project’s public status remains exactly what it was when announced: proposed.

Where Laredo’s government stands

In August, the Laredo City Council opted against a moratorium on data centers and instead directed staff to develop a permanent regulatory framework — learning in the process that city code simply prohibits uses that aren’t specifically permitted.

Water is the live issue. At the May 18 council meeting, a coalition calling itself “Fronteras and Data Centers” warned the project could demand millions of gallons of water in a region already facing long-term water insecurity — while residents in colonias still haul water. Speakers demanded transparency, asking that no city official sign nondisclosure agreements tied to the development. Council Member Dr. Tyler King clarified that the proposed site is outside city limits and that no city discussions with the developer had taken place.

What the mayoral candidates say — and don’t

Webb Watch’s October 18 investigation found that JD Gonzalez’s six-plank platform never mentions data centers at all — notable for a candidate whose pitch is trade and economic expertise. Voter-guide summaries describe Alfonso “Poncho” Casso’s campaign as centered on accountability, transparency, water security, and international trade. Dr. Victor Treviño, as mayor, has presided over the standards-over-moratorium approach — the city chose regulation rather than a ban. We found no detailed public position from Alyssa Cigarroa or Jorge A. Garza on the project.

What Webb Watch 956 is asking

  • Has Energy Abundance filed any permit with TCEQ, the county, or the state? Oil and Gas Watch will be monitoring; so will we.
  • Where exactly does the water come from — and who gets it first in a drought: residents or servers?
  • What does “100% green energy” mean in 2026 if the first 300 MW runs on natural gas turbines? (Answer: it’s the long-term plan, not the starting fuel. The marketing should say so.)
  • What jobs, and on what timeline? 2026 was the company’s target year for phase one. Voters deserve to know what exists on the ground today.

Five gigawatts is an enormous bet on Webb County’s land, water, and energy future. The watchdog will keep checking what’s real.

Update — October 20, 2026

On the statewide permit question: TCEQ's public records show the state kept moving data-center permits forward after Governor Greg Abbott's September 21 directive to halt them, according to an October 19 analysis of the agency's database by Public Citizen and FracTracker Alliance, reported by Inside Climate News and 404 Media. The groups identified 35 permitting actions taken after the directive — including reviews of gas-plant applications and construction stormwater approvals. Abbott's office disputes that characterization, telling 404 Media that no permits were approved. None of the permitting actions reported named Energy Abundance's Data City project; whether the company has filed anything with TCEQ remains the open question this story is tracking.
